section_summary: This section covers Japan’s automobile manufacturing policy, its limits on American assembly plants, and the progress of Nissan and Datsun production. Consular reports and State Department memoranda compare Japanese production claims with Ford and General Motors operations, especially after the outbreak of war in China. The section ends partway through a confidential 1939 report on Japan’s automotive industry.

subfiles.title: Treaty analysis of proposed Japanese automobile legislation
subfiles.about: The concluding page distinguishes treaty rights of American citizens from claims on behalf of American corporations.
subfiles.summary: Concludes that a U.S. protest should defend American citizens’ ownership rights in Japanese automobile companies.

subfiles.title: Comment on Tokyo despatch concerning proposed automobile legislation
subfiles.about: The memorandum assesses Japan’s interpretation of the 1911 treaty and recommends clarifying U.S. opposition to ownership restrictions.
subfiles.summary: Reviews the Japanese Vice Minister’s position and argues that excluding American citizens from majority ownership of Japanese automobile companies would raise a treaty issue.

subfiles.title: Japanese Automobile Industry
subfiles.from: Richard F. Boyce, American Consul, Yokohama
subfiles.about: Boyce reports on Nissan’s new standard sized car, its American equipment, production prospects, and Datsun output.
subfiles.summary: Nissan displayed passenger, truck, and bus models assembled initially from Graham-Paige parts. Boyce describes high costs, imported materials, limited skilled labor, and expected protection against American cars. He also reports conflicting estimates of Datsun production.

subfiles.title: The Japan Advertiser Nissan automobile coverage
subfiles.about: Newspaper pages announce Nissan’s new car and include automotive history, driving rules, advertisements, and other motoring news.
subfiles.summary: The principal article describes Nissan’s move from Datsun small cars to full size passenger cars, trucks, and buses, with government support and expanded factory and sales operations. Associated pages give photographs, production figures, driving license guidance, motoring news, and advertisements.

subfiles.title: Announcing the Japan Made Nissan Motorcar
subfiles.about: A four page advertisement announces a May 29–31 showing and specifications for Nissan passenger, truck, and bus models.
subfiles.summary: Promotes Nissan’s new models and lists engine, chassis, dimensions, and sales information.

subfiles.title: Ford imports above its assembly quota
subfiles.about: The memorandum notes Ford’s imports of assembled vehicles beyond its quota and expected future restrictions.
subfiles.summary: Ford imported 3,600 complete units beyond its assembly quota and ordered 3,000 more amid military demand.

subfiles.title: Position of the Ford Motor Company vis-à-vis the Automobile Industry Control Law
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew reports that Embassy staff explained the Department’s position to Ford manager Benjamin Kopf.
subfiles.summary: Forwards a memorandum of the Embassy’s conversation with Kopf about Ford’s position under Japanese automobile controls.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Benjamin Kopf
subfiles.from: McGurk, First Secretary of the Embassy
subfiles.about: Kopf discusses Ford’s imported units, possible increased military production, and likely renewed restrictions.
subfiles.summary: Kopf says Ford’s imports of complete vehicles do not violate its assembly quota. He describes an inquiry about doubling daily output, a further order from Detroit, and his expectation that Japan will again restrict Ford after the emergency.

subfiles.title: Comment on Yokohama despatch about the automotive industry
subfiles.about: The memorandum highlights claims that Nissan was failing while Ford’s business was strong.
subfiles.summary: Highlights Boyce’s report of low Nissan output and a Ford manager’s expectation of liberalized controls.

subfiles.title: Automotive Industry of Japan
subfiles.from: Richard F. Boyce, American Consul, Yokohama
subfiles.about: Boyce reports Nissan production and conveys a Ford manager’s assessment of Nissan and Japanese controls.
subfiles.summary: A Graham-Paige engineer describes Nissan’s imported parts, uneven plant capacity, labor, and materials. Boyce reports production of about 20 Nissan and 35 Datsun vehicles daily, alongside a competitor’s claim that the Nissan venture was failing.

subfiles.title: File note on American automobile assembly plants
subfiles.about: The note points to a report on American and Japanese automobile production in Japan.
subfiles.summary: References a report noting American vehicles’ dominance and some success by Japanese manufacturers.

subfiles.title: File note on mass production of automobiles in Japan
subfiles.from: E. P. Thomas, National Foreign Trade Council
subfiles.about: The note points to a letter conveying Count Kabayama’s proposal for expanded Ford production with Japanese capital.
subfiles.summary: References Kabayama’s view that Ford should expand Japanese production with local capital for regional sales.

subfiles.title: Inquiry into reported Japanese purchase of American automobiles
subfiles.about: The memorandum records the Commerce Department’s view that a reported purchase was unfounded.
subfiles.summary: Commerce officials doubt the reported purchase and consider credit financed truck sales unlikely.

subfiles.title: Rumor of purchase by Japanese interests in Manchuria of American motor trucks
subfiles.from: Hamilton, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: General Motors representative Roberts asks about a rumored American truck order for Japanese interests in Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Roberts relays an unconfirmed New York rumor that Dowa ordered American trucks through Asahara with American financing. Hamilton says the Department has no information and will inquire.

subfiles.title: Comment on Allison’s report, Japan’s Automotive Industry and the China Incident
subfiles.from: Jones, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: The memorandum critiques Allison’s production estimates and compares his report with Boyce’s assessment.
subfiles.summary: Jones summarizes prewar production, American assembly quotas, imports, and Japanese plans. He questions reports of rapid Japanese growth and self sufficiency, stresses the continued need for imported vehicles and parts, and finds Boyce’s more skeptical assessment more realistic.

subfiles.title: Japan’s Automotive Industry and the China Incident
subfiles.about: The opening of Allison’s report traces Japan’s automobile industry and wartime restrictions on American producers.
subfiles.summary: The report presents historical registration, production, import, and export figures, then describes the 1936 automobile law and quotas on Ford and General Motors. It cites a three year plan for Japanese self sufficiency and estimated growth at Nissan and Toyoda. The pages provided end amid a discussion of exchange permits, reduced American assembly output, and restrictions on passenger car imports.
